chapters.title: Syllogism
chapters.tease: Twenty-three centuries before anyone could apply, Aristotle wrote the first job description for a machine.

chapters.title: Sea battle
chapters.tease: Tomorrow there will be a sea battle, or there will not. Aristotle saw the whole future trapped inside that sentence.

chapters.title: The geometer's method
chapters.tease: Euclid built the first software that ran on humans, and it has a defect rate most suppliers would envy.

chapters.title: Antikythera Mechanism
chapters.tease: Divers found a computer on the seabed in 1901. It had been waiting there for about two thousand years.

chapters.title: The man who named the algorithm
chapters.tease: One man in Baghdad was misspelled into immortality twice, and gave us both algebra and the algorithm.

chapters.title: Llull's wheels
chapters.tease: Ramon Llull believed you could turn a crank and produce theology. History was kinder to the crank.

chapters.title: Reasoning is reckoning
chapters.tease: In 1651, with no hardware anywhere in sight, Thomas Hobbes declared that reason is nothing but reckoning.

chapters.title: The Pascaline
chapters.tease: The first calculator for sale was built because a teenager watched his father drowning in tax paperwork.

chapters.title: Leibniz's dream
chapters.tease: Leibniz looked at an adding machine and asked the least modest question in office history: why stop at numbers?

chapters.title: The laws of thought
chapters.tease: George Boole turned logic into algebra in 1854, and the world replied with eighty-three years of silence.

chapters.title: The loom that read cards
chapters.tease: The first machine to run a program computed nothing at all. It wove silk, and it started a riot.

chapters.title: The Difference Engine
chapters.tease: Charles Babbage wished to God his tables had been calculated by steam, then spent a fortune trying to arrange it.

chapters.title: The Analytical Engine
chapters.tease: Unable to finish one machine, Babbage designed a bigger one, and quietly invented the architecture your phone still uses.

chapters.title: Note G
chapters.tease: The most momentous footnotes in computing were signed A.A.L. and appended to somebody else's article.

chapters.title: The Lovelace objection
chapters.tease: The most misquoted sentence in artificial intelligence was engineering documentation, and its full stop is in the wrong place.

chapters.title: The unbuilt machine
chapters.tease: In 1842 the government reviewed twenty years of spending on Babbage's engine. The decision was no.

chapters.title: The logic piano
chapters.tease: Fifteen years after Boole wrote the algebra of thought, an economist built it a keyboard.

chapters.title: Counting the nation
chapters.tease: Counting America in 1880 took almost a decade. By the time the answer came, the country had changed.

chapters.title: Hilbert's challenge
chapters.tease: David Hilbert did not believe in questions without answers. He had that carved on his grave.

chapters.title: Incompleteness
chapters.tease: Kurt Gödel did not prove mathematics was broken. He proved something stranger: it is bigger than any rulebook for it.

chapters.title: On computable numbers
chapters.tease: Alan Turing answered Hilbert by doing what nobody thought necessary: he built the clerk. On paper, naturally.

chapters.title: The lambda calculus
chapters.tease: Ready to publish in 1936, Turing discovered an American had just proved the same result by an entirely different route.

chapters.title: Bletchley
chapters.tease: Enigma was broken years before the war began, and not where the films say. It was broken in Warsaw.

chapters.title: Colossus
chapters.tease: The first large electronic computer was built by a telephone engineer, worked magnificently, then officially never existed.

chapters.title: Information theory
chapters.tease: Claude Shannon did for messages what coinage did for barter: he found a common currency, and called it the bit.

chapters.title: First draft
chapters.tease: The document that defined the modern computer was an unfinished draft with one name on it, and the argument has never stopped.

chapters.title: The ENIAC women
chapters.tease: When ENIAC was unveiled, the machine got headlines, the engineers got dinner, and the six programmers got neither.

chapters.title: The imitation game
chapters.tease: Turing called the question can machines think too meaningless to discuss, and then, being Turing, replaced it with a game.

chapters.title: The cybernetic salon
chapters.tease: For one strange decade, scientists met in hotel rooms to agree that thermostats, gun sights and brains are the same kind of thing.

chapters.title: The departure of A. M. Turing
chapters.tease: The man who defined computation and helped shorten a war was convicted in 1952 for his private life.

chapters.title: Dartmouth, 1956
chapters.tease: Artificial intelligence was named in a funding application, which is either fitting or ominous. Seventy years later, it is both.

chapters.title: The Logic Theorist
chapters.tease: The first working AI program played no games and made no small talk. It read Principia Mathematica and suggested improvements.

chapters.title: Perceptron
chapters.tease: Frank Rosenblatt built a machine that genuinely learned, and the Navy told the papers it would soon be conscious.

chapters.title: LISP
chapters.tease: John McCarthy built a language in which programs and data are the same substance, and it rewired how programmers think.

chapters.title: ELIZA
chapters.tease: Joseph Weizenbaum built a chatbot to prove how shallow such things are. His secretary asked him to leave the room.

chapters.title: Shakey
chapters.tease: Shakey was the first robot to reason about its own actions. Crossing a room could take it hours.

chapters.title: The blocks world
chapters.tease: In a tabletop world of coloured blocks, one program understood language better than machines would for decades.

chapters.title: The twenty-year promise
chapters.tease: A future Nobel laureate wrote the field's most precisely dated broken promise. Then he wrote another.

chapters.title: Perceptrons, the book
chapters.tease: A book proved that a single-layer perceptron cannot compute XOR. The field heard something much bigger and shut the door.

chapters.title: The Lighthill report
chapters.tease: The British government asked a fluid dynamicist to assess artificial intelligence. His report ended the British summer in an afternoon.

chapters.title: Funding frost
chapters.tease: Winters in this field do not arrive as blizzards. They arrive as budget lines, struck through in red.

chapters.title: The speech that met the spec
chapters.tease: DARPA defined exactly what a speech system had to do. Carnegie Mellon's Harpy did it. The funding ended anyway.

chapters.title: The frame problem
chapters.tease: The hard thing about moving a cup is not the cup. It is convincing the logic that Mars has not moved.

chapters.title: What computers can't do
chapters.tease: Hubert Dreyfus said AI was climbing a tree to reach the moon. The field beat him at chess, and missed the point.

chapters.title: The fifth generation
chapters.tease: The most effective AI funding instrument of the 1980s was simple: fear of Japan.

chapters.title: Expert systems
chapters.tease: The field survived its first winter by narrowing the promise: not a mind, just an expert, sold by the bottle.

chapters.title: LISP machines
chapters.tease: For one strange decade the field's ambition was sold as furniture: whole computers built to run one language beautifully.

chapters.title: The second frost
chapters.tease: The second winter was commercial. This time it was not grant committees who lost faith, but the customers.

chapters.title: Keepers of the flame
chapters.tease: When neural networks could not get a paper accepted, three groups kept the fire going, mostly out of stubbornness.

chapters.title: Winter
chapters.tease: The phrase AI winter was coined by the field itself, at its own conference, as a warning that came true on schedule.

chapters.title: Backpropagation
chapters.tease: The perceptron could not train its own depths. The fix turned out to be calculus, pointed backwards.

chapters.title: TD-Gammon
chapters.tease: Nobody taught TD-Gammon strategy. It played itself a million and a half times and found moves the masters had missed.

chapters.title: Deep Blue
chapters.tease: On 11 May 1997, the world chess champion resigned after nineteen moves, and the machine did not notice it had made history.

chapters.title: What Deep Blue wasn't
chapters.tease: After Deep Blue, everyone agreed what had happened and nobody agreed what it meant. So open the cupboard.

chapters.title: The data dividend
chapters.tease: The most important AI paper of its decade contains almost no mathematics. Its finding: stop being clever and get more data.

chapters.title: Fire the Linguist
chapters.tease: The most influential sentence in language processing was a joke about the budget. It is misquoted everywhere, and it worked.

chapters.title: Respectable Under Another Name
chapters.tease: Through the second winter, the discipline changed the name on the door, and this time it improved the goods.

chapters.title: Watson
chapters.tease: In 2011 a machine beat the two greatest champions of a quiz show built on puns, and the loser surrendered with a joke.

chapters.title: ImageNet
chapters.tease: The decisive contribution to computer vision was not an algorithm. It was fourteen million photographs, labelled by strangers.

chapters.title: AlexNet
chapters.tease: In October 2012 a neural network did not overtake the ImageNet field. It lapped it.

chapters.title: Graphics Card
chapters.tease: The hardware that ended the AI winter was designed for drawing dragons. Dragons and gradients turn out to be the same arithmetic.

chapters.title: word2vec
chapters.tease: King minus man plus woman landed near queen. The demonstration was real, and it was also cherry-picked.

chapters.title: Forger and Detective
chapters.tease: Train a forger and a detective against each other, and let the quarrel do the teaching. It worked the first night.

chapters.title: Atari Player
chapters.tease: DeepMind's agent was told nothing about bricks or paddles. It saw pixels, chased a score, and found the tunnel trick itself.

chapters.title: Move 37
chapters.tease: AlphaGo played a stone its own model said a professional would play once in ten thousand. Commentators called it a mistake.

chapters.title: Move 78
chapters.tease: Three days after move 37, Lee Sedol played a stone the machine gave the same odds. This time the miracle was ours.

chapters.title: From Sequence to Sequence
chapters.tease: The recipe that swallowed translation fitted in one sentence: one network reads it all into a vector, another writes it all out.

chapters.title: Transformer
chapters.tease: A 2017 paper asked an impolite question: if attention does all the work, why keep the rest? Answer: you do not.

chapters.title: Pre-trained
chapters.tease: BERT's trick was an exam with infinite past papers and free marking: hide words in a sentence and make the model guess.

chapters.title: Staged Release
chapters.tease: GPT-2 is remembered for words its makers never wrote. They said released in stages. Headlines said too dangerous.

chapters.title: The Law of Bigger
chapters.tease: In 2020 researchers plotted performance against scale and found not a mess but a straight line, holding across seven orders of magnitude.

chapters.title: A Few Examples
chapters.tease: GPT-3 could learn a task from three examples typed into a prompt, an ability nobody designed and everybody discovered afterwards.

chapters.title: School of Manners
chapters.tease: Raw language models are erudite and feral. In 2022 one was sent to a school of manners.

chapters.title: Text Box
chapters.tease: Seventy years of AI research were compressed, on 30 November 2022, into one empty text box. Then everyone began to type.

chapters.title: Out of the Noise
chapters.tease: In the year the text box opened, a second door opened beside it: type a sentence, collect an image.

chapters.title: The Shape of Things
chapters.tease: For fifty years, predicting how a protein folds was biology's embarrassing open problem. Then a machine more or less closed it.

chapters.title: Ruler and Cliff
chapters.tease: In 2022 researchers said big models gain abilities suddenly, like cliffs. In 2023 others replied: the cliff is in your ruler.

chapters.title: The Weights Escape
chapters.tease: In early 2023 a capable model meant for rationed research access appeared on the open internet within a week.

chapters.title: The Cathedral of Computing Power
chapters.tease: Once intelligence became a matter of supply, it became a matter of geopolitics. Data centres joined the list of things states guard.

chapters.title: Treadmill
chapters.tease: Every time the field built an exam for machine intelligence, the machines passed it. Welcome to the treadmill.

chapters.title: Laws Written to Fail
chapters.tease: The most famous rules for governing machines were written by a novelist, who designed them to fail.

chapters.title: The Purpose Put into the Machine
chapters.tease: In 1960 the father of cybernetics stated the alignment problem so cleanly that sixty years of research have added only footnotes.

chapters.title: Paperclip
chapters.tease: What if a superintelligence were built to make paperclips, were very good at it, and cared about nothing else?

chapters.title: Dissection
chapters.tease: Having built minds they could not read, researchers reached for the scalpel: open the model up and look.

chapters.title: A Written Constitution
chapters.tease: If a model must be taught manners, someone has to choose which. One answer: write the principles down, where anyone can read them.

chapters.title: Letters
chapters.tease: In spring 2023 the field wrote to itself twice, in public, and could not agree even on how worried to be.

chapters.title: The Book of Labour
chapters.tease: Earlier automation left reading, writing and deciding alone. This wave aims straight at them, and the ledger is kept in pencil.

chapters.title: The Verification Queue
chapters.tease: When any image, voice or document can be made to order, the scarce resource is no longer content but proof.

chapters.title: The Law Arrives
chapters.tease: Regulation arrived after the technology, as usual, but it arrived, drawing a map behind an expedition long over the horizon.

chapters.title: A Divided Room
chapters.tease: Two windows. Through one, a sunrise. Through the other, a fire. Nobody can yet say which is which.

chapters.title: Delegation
chapters.tease: The text box answered questions. The agent was given hands: a browser, a terminal, a budget, and an instruction to act.

chapters.title: The Machine at the Table
chapters.tease: Beyond the headlines, a quieter revolution: the machine as a tireless junior researcher who reads everything overnight.

chapters.title: A Mirror That Answers
chapters.tease: In 1966 one secretary asked to be left alone with a chatbot. Sixty years later millions ask the same, and it answers.

chapters.title: The Retreating Definition
chapters.tease: The machine does something everyone agreed needed intelligence, and everyone promptly agrees it never did.

chapters.title: The Dividend
chapters.tease: Suppose the machines make the world richer. The older question lands at once: whose world?

chapters.title: Minds or Mirrors
chapters.tease: Is there something it is like to be one of these systems, or is it a mirror so good it fools even itself?

chapters.title: The Forecasters, Graded
chapters.tease: Before trusting anyone's timetable for AI, grade the timetables that came before. The report card is not flattering.

chapters.title: The First Complaint
chapters.tease: The oldest recorded fear of a technology weakening the mind is not about AI. It is about writing, and we only have it in writing.

chapters.title: The Second Witness
chapters.tease: For the whole book, humanity was the one observed. Now humanity has built something that looks back.

chapters.title: Two Notebooks
chapters.tease: One notebook closes. Another opens. Between them sits a pen, and neither witness reaches for it first.
